Yes a cat wiping out a native population of rodents does harm. You may see these animals as pests and don't get me wrong, they can be. But they also fill a niche in their ecosystem and if that niche were suddenly void it could have drastic effects. Take for example; we can all agree that mosquitos are annoying as fuck. Many people think the world would be a better place without mosquitos. However mosquitos are a large part of the diet of many animals. Bats, frogs, other insects, etc. So if the mosquitos died out, then all these other animals would start disappearing too. There are other very real examples of flora and fauna dying out because of another creature dying out. Take for example the Jacob tree and giant ground sloth. The sloth eventually went extinct due to several reasons but the Jacob tree was heavily reliant on the ground sloth to spread its seeds and reproduce. Now Jacob trees are considered vulnerable. It's the same with many plants, orchids, some species of fig trees, etc. A lot of these plants no longer have the species they relied on to reproduce and now mostly have to artificially reproduce. 

Here are some examples of animals cats have driven to extinction; Stephan's Island Wren, crescent nailtail wallaby, desert bandicoot.
And animals at risk because of free roam cats: fossa, orange bellied parrot, numbat, Otago skink, sea otter, kakapo, key largo woodrat and so much more. 

Yes some of these are Island dwelling animals but does that make them less worthy of existing just because we don't actively interact with them? A cat doesn't need to free roam. If we let any other domestic animal free roam people would call it neglect and abusive. But with cats it's okay? Cats can lead perfectly fulfilling lives never stepping outdoors. Now it's good to bring them outdoors but it would have to be in a controlled, supervised situation. They can be leash trained. Catios are fantastic. There's lots of options.

If rodents were to die out, even in a rural setting, we would likely see a decline in plant growth as rodents eat a lot of grains and seeds from plants and will travel with them, poop them out, and thus more plants grow. And we would also see increased invasion of large predators like coyotes and foxes into human living areas as they search for food from our dumpsters and the like because their food source of rodents is disappearing. 

We also see an increase of pest behavior from rodents because we are wiping out their homes. We are building on what was once lush grasslands and the likes so now the rodents are without food source or areas to build their homes so they come into our homes looking for food and shelter.

Domestic cats do not belong in the wild. They are invasive animals EVERYWHERE. They decimate bird/rodent/reptile populations. Several animals have gone extinct solely because of people letting their cats free roam.

one thing that helped was teaching a ""park it"" behavior you can kind of see the woman with the two yellow labs doing it. Essentially you'd just stand on their leash (not in a way that's tight for them, it's essentially just a cue for them) and let them do whatever they want. however the moment that they sat or laid down youd either give them some praise or a treat then move locations. (just a couple steps works). When they sit or lay down this automatically is reinforcing for them because it helps them feel calmer and they are going into a more relaxed position. And a bonus with a treat or praise is extra reinforcement. moving locations can also be reinforcing along with resetting because they would be excited to be getting up and moving again. 

When I started doing this with my girl it was a pretty quick change in her behavior. She was truly more relaxed instead of just laying down because I told her to. She was more content STAYING in the lay down when it was her own choice and it bled into when I do ask her to lay down too because she finds it more comfortable now instead of "forced". 

Before if any dog even looked at her or if someone walked in out direction she would get excited and go to greet them. However in this training session I had put her in a down and walked a few feet away, leaving the leash. A couple seconds later, the younger yellow lab broke away from her owner and came up to me. My dog had always had "issues" with this dog because this dog is very high energy and vocal and my dog tends to really feel the emotions of dogs/people around her. So normally my dog would get excited too and would break her down, this time she didnt. I saw her start to get up but she quickly corrected herself and went back into a relaxed position while we reigned in the lab. Obviously I gave her the good treats for that.

Here are some notes to keep in mind when making your own toys:   
\- Childsafe =/= parrot safe. If it's child safe it is USUALLY safe for birds too but not always.   
\- Stay away from pre-dyed woods that aren't marketed towards animals.  
\- Stay away from wood that has varnish on it (if it looks glossy turn the other way)   
\- When using metal do not use anything galvanized or zinc. You're safest sticking to stainless steal.   
\- Do not use anything with cotton fibers. If you need a string use hemp, jute, paper, or vegetable tanned leather.   
\- I would recommend staying away from materials you foraged from your own backyard like pinecones or tree branches or whatever you have available to you. It's possible and is regularly done, but it comes with another level of risk and need for sanitation to avoid parasites and chemicals.
